items.prompt: A dashboard keeps yesterday's readings array and passes it to capReadings(readings, max), which caps every reading at max. Afterwards the dashboard compares yesterday's array with the returned array to highlight which readings changed. Should capReadings change the array in place (readings[i] = Math.min(readings[i], max)) or build a new array? Justify your choice from what the caller needs, and describe one test that would catch the wrong choice.
items.answer: Build and return a new array, for example with readings.map(r => Math.min(r, max)) or a loop that pushes into a fresh array. The caller still needs the original values for its comparison. Capping in place would change the very array the caller holds, because the parameter and the caller's variable refer to the same array, so the comparison would find no differences. A test: call capReadings([3, 12], 10), check the result is [3, 10], and check that the input array is still [3, 12].
items.explanation: The caller's later comparison is the requirement that decides the contract: in-place updates are only safe when no one else needs the old values.

items.explanation: Only interior positions are compared with both neighbours, using strict comparisons, so ends, plateaus and short arrays give no peaks.

items.prompt: A class method uses this.name. After the code passes it as a callback, `button.onClick(user.greet)`, the method fails because it no longer sees the user. In your own words, why does that happen, and name one way to fix it.
items.answer: The value of this depends on how a function is called, not where it was defined. Passing user.greet hands over the bare function, which is later called plainly rather than as user.greet(), so this is undefined (strict mode) or the global object instead of user. Fix it by binding the method (user.greet.bind(user)) or wrapping it in an arrow function that calls user.greet().

items.prompt: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 9]`. Explain why, and what you change to get numeric ascending order.
items.answer: Without a comparator, sort converts every element to a string and compares them as text, character by character (UTF-16 code units), so '10' comes before '9' because '1' is less than '9'. Pass a comparator such as (a, b) => a - b to compare them as numbers.

items.prompt: A click handler runs a synchronous loop that takes three seconds. The user clicks another button during those three seconds. What happens?
choices: The second click runs immediately, between iterations of the loop
The second click's handler runs on a second JavaScript thread
The second click's handler waits until the loop has finished
The second click is discarded and never delivered
items.explanation: JavaScript jobs run to completion on one thread. The event waits in the task queue until the running code returns.

items.prompt: A microtask keeps scheduling another microtask, forever. What happens to a pending setTimeout(fn, 0) callback?
choices: It runs between microtasks, because timers have higher priority
It runs after a short delay, once the browser clamps the microtasks
It runs as soon as the queue holds more than ten microtasks
It never runs, because microtasks are drained first
items.explanation: After each task the host drains the microtask queue, including microtasks added while draining, so the timer task starves.

items.prompt: In what order are the letters printed?

items.prompt: Type exactly what this prints (seven tokens separated by single spaces).
items.answer: S M1 Q M3 M2 T1 T2
items.explanation: Synchronous code first, then all microtasks in FIFO order (a microtask added while draining still runs before any timer; M2 is queued only after M1 finishes, behind M3), then the timers in order.

items.prompt: A search function is declared `async` and contains a long CPU-heavy loop. While it runs, the page becomes unresponsive. A teammate says 'it's async, so it can't hold anything up'. Explain why that is wrong and how you could fix it.
items.answer: Async functions still run on the single JavaScript thread and run to completion until they hit an await on something pending. A long synchronous loop keeps the thread busy, so no other task, timer, input event or rendering can run until it returns. Fix it by splitting the work into chunks and yielding between them (for example with a timer), or by moving it into a worker.

items.prompt: An async function's body throws an Error before its first await. What does calling the function return?
choices: A promise that is rejected with that error
Nothing: the error is thrown synchronously at the call
undefined, and the error is silently dropped
A fulfilled promise whose value is the Error object
items.explanation: An async function always returns a promise; a thrown error rejects it instead of propagating synchronously.

items.prompt: Which lines are printed, in order?
items.code:
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then(v => { throw new Error('bad' + v); })
  .then(() => console.log('skipped'))
  .catch(e => { console.log(e.message); return 'recovered'; })
  .then(v => console.log(v))
  .finally(() => console.log('done'));
items.explanation: The throw skips the next then, catch handles it and returns a value, the next then prints the recovered value, and finally runs last.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this prints (separated by single spaces).
items.answer: true function sync caught x try x after
items.explanation: The async function returns a promise immediately; 'sync' prints before any reaction. The rejection handlers then run as microtasks in the order they were registered; await throws at the await so try/catch handles it.

items.prompt: fetch('/missing') reaches the server, which answers with HTTP 404. What does the returned promise do?
choices: It rejects with an HTTPError object that carries status 404
It rejects with a TypeError describing the failed request
It throws synchronously at the call, before any promise exists
It fulfills with a Response whose ok is false
items.explanation: fetch rejects for network and abort failures; an HTTP error status still resolves to a Response, so check response.ok before parsing.

items.prompt: An async function is paused at an await on a promise that is still pending. What happens to the rest of the program?
choices: Every other piece of code waits until that promise settles
Other code keeps running; the function resumes once it settles
The function is cancelled if the promise takes longer than the current task
The JavaScript engine starts a second thread to run the rest of the program
items.explanation: await suspends only that async function's continuation; the thread is free to run other work.

items.prompt: Three requests are started and combined with Promise.all. One of them fails straight away. Does the code stop the other two? Explain, and say what real cancellation would need.
items.answer: No. Promise.all just settles early with the first failure; it does not cancel the other operations, which keep running and whose results are ignored. Real cancellation has to be supported by the underlying API, typically by passing an AbortSignal from an AbortController to each request.

items.prompt: controller.abort() is called with no argument. What is controller.signal.reason afterwards?
items.explanation: Without an argument the reason is a DOMException named AbortError (TimeoutError is for AbortSignal.timeout).

items.prompt: Type exactly what this prints (two output lines, written on one line separated by a single space).
items.explanation: abort() is idempotent: the abort event fires once and the reason is the default AbortError.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this prints (separated by single spaces).

items.explanation: A custom reason is stored as given; throwIfAborted throws that reason on an aborted signal and does nothing otherwise.

items.prompt: Type exactly what this prints (three values separated by single spaces).
items.explanation: AbortSignal.any aborts as soon as any input aborts, with that input's reason; the 10 ms timeout signal has not fired yet.

items.explanation: Aborting fires the event but does not interrupt the loop: nothing in it checks the signal, so all three iterations run.

items.prompt: A request was cancelled with controller.abort(). The user retries. What is the correct way to get a fresh cancellable request?
choices: Call controller.reset() and reuse the same controller
Create a new AbortController for the new request
Call controller.abort() once more to toggle it back
items.explanation: Aborting is one-way and a controller cannot be reset; create a new controller (and signal) per operation.

items.prompt: A teammate calls controller.abort() to stop a function that runs a long synchronous loop and never looks at the controller. They expect the loop to stop. Does it, and what must the function do for cancellation to work? Does aborting also undo work that has already been done?
items.answer: No. Cancellation is cooperative: the loop only stops if it checks the signal (signal.aborted or throwIfAborted) between chunks or listens for the abort event and then rejects or throws. Aborting does not undo side effects already performed, such as a request the server already processed.

items.prompt: In Node.js, which file name is treated as an ES module regardless of what package.json says?
items.explanation: .mjs is always ESM and .cjs always CommonJS; .js depends on the package's "type" field.

items.explanation: An imported binding is a live read-only view of the exported variable, not a copy, so it reflects the increments.

items.prompt: This runs a tiny ES module from a data: URL. Type exactly what it prints (two numbers separated by a space).
items.explanation: `copy` is an ordinary copy made at that moment (0); m.n is the live exported binding (2 after two inc() calls).

items.prompt: This also imports a module from a data: URL. Type exactly what it prints (two output lines, written on one line separated by a single space).
items.explanation: import() returns a promise immediately; the module namespace arrives later with the named and default exports.

items.prompt: `import { walk } from './graph'` works in your Vite dev server but fails under plain Node.js ESM with a module-not-found error. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Static import syntax is only allowed in browsers and bundlers, not in Node.js at all
The bundler rewrote the import into a dynamic import() call that Node.js rejects
Node ESM needs a file extension on relative paths, which the bundler let you omit
walk has to be exported as a default export before Node.js can find it
items.explanation: Bundlers accept extensionless specifiers and aliases that Node's ESM resolver does not; write './graph.js'.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT available inside an ES module in Node.js?
items.explanation: In ESM, __dirname, __filename and require are not defined; use import.meta.url (or import.meta.dirname in recent Node.js).

items.prompt: How does a dynamic import() differ from a top-level `import ... from` declaration, and when would you choose it?
items.answer: A top-level import is resolved and linked before the importing module's body runs, so everything it names is ready up front. import() returns a promise for the module namespace, loading on demand at run time, so you use it to load code conditionally or lazily, and you must handle a rejected promise.
